nutshell: Systems with LiDAR sensors have no established methods for object re-identification the way camera-based person/vehicle ReID does. This paper runs the first large-scale study of object ReID directly from real point clouds: it builds two new paired image+LiDAR ReID datasets from nuScenes and the Waymo Open Dataset, proposes RTMM (a lightweight, symmetric, real-time matching head attachable to any point-processing backbone), and shows point-cloud ReID performance climbs toward (but doesn't yet match) image-based ReID as LiDAR sensor resolution/point density increases.
contributions: RTMM: a symmetric real-time matching head (adapted from a single-object-tracking model's Coarse-to-Fine Correlation Network) that attaches to any point or sequence backbone (PointNet, DGCNN, Point-Transformer, or even ViT-style image patch sequences), letting each input play query and key/value in turn - runs thousands of pairwise comparisons at 10Hz and beats the original asymmetric matching head on both accuracy and inference speed.

Two new large-scale point-cloud ReID datasets built from nuScenes (32-beam LiDAR) and Waymo Open Dataset (64-beam+ LiDAR), with paired image/LiDAR object crops extracted via realistic 3D object detectors (not ground-truth boxes), plus an 'Even Sampling' training algorithm that matches the point-density distribution of negative pairs to positive pairs, avoiding a spurious point-count-as-identity shortcut - improving every backbone tested by 1.4-2.7 accuracy points.

The first systematic head-to-head comparison of point-cloud vs. image ReID across sensor resolutions and object classes, showing point-cloud ReID's performance gap to image ReID shrinks substantially with denser LiDAR, and that even deformable objects (pedestrians) can be re-identified reasonably well directly from shape alone, without any explicit skeleton/pose normalization, once point density is high enough.

A power-law extrapolation (fit to models trained at 400/800/1600/3200 epochs) projecting that an order of magnitude more training compute could push their strongest model's error below 9% (i.e. >91% accuracy), beyond their actual compute budget.
deficiencies: The headline claim that increased LiDAR resolution (not just more training data) drives the point-ReID improvement from nuScenes to Waymo is confounded - Waymo also has 80% more training objects - and the paper resolves this with a rough back-of-envelope subtraction (12.45% total gain minus a 5.07% image-model gain = 7.38% attributed to resolution) rather than a controlled ablation that holds dataset size fixed while varying only point density.

Despite the framing that 'point cloud ReID approaches image ReID', the primary comparison table (Table 2) shows image models outperforming point models on every single metric on both nuScenes Eval and Waymo Eval - the 'approaches' claim holds only in the density-conditioned analysis of Figure 1 (comparing only observations above a point-count threshold), not in the main reported accuracy numbers.

The deformable-object success story is real but overstated in absolute terms: even on the best Waymo results, pedestrian accuracy (82.94%, base model; 86.22% at 3200 epochs) trails rigid classes like car (88.84% / 90.68%) and truck (88.58% / 90.92%) by 5-6 points, a persistent gap the 'no explicit skeleton normalization needed' framing doesn't fully reconcile.

The forward-looking compute-scaling claim (projected <9% error with 10x more training) rests on a power-law fit to only four data points (400, 800, 1600, 3200 epochs) for a single architecture (Point-Transformer) on one dataset (WOD) - a thin empirical basis for what the abstract presents as a general finding about the method's scalability.
notable: The 'Even Sampling' fix is a simple, broadly reusable trick for any point-cloud (or other variable-density) matching/retrieval setup: naively sampling negative pairs uniformly lets models learn a shortcut where point count itself (rather than shape) predicts identity, since positive pairs of the same object tend to share similar point densities; resampling negatives to match the density distribution of positives closes that shortcut and measurably improves every backbone tested. Also notable: the datasets are built directly from a real object-detector's noisy predicted boxes (not ground truth), so the benchmark reflects realistic tracking-by-detection noise rather than an idealized setting.
